methodology: The study involved constructing three cantilever column specimens without incorporating modern design code requirements for seismic safety and structural integrity. The specimens were then strengthened using either carbon fiber-reinforced polymer textile wrapping or thin high-strength reinforced concrete jackets, with the length of lap splices and amount of confinement provided by the jackets being examined as main variables.
research_objective: To experimentally and analytically investigate the effectiveness of two different strengthening systems (carbon fiber-reinforced polymer textile wrapping or thin high-strength reinforced concrete jackets) for seismic retrofitting of RC columns, with the length of lap splices and amount of confinement provided by the jackets being examined as main variables.

key_findings.finding: The effectiveness of CFRP jackets and thin high-strength RC jackets for seismic retrofitting of RC columns was experimentally and analytically investigated.

The specimens were subjected to earthquake-type loading, their hysteretic performances compared, and the behavior of a control specimen with continuous reinforcement in a previous study was also evaluated.
CFRP strengthening technique can improve seismic behavior of RC structures, but requires proper design to ensure ductile performance.
WRAPPING OF CFRP TEXTILE AROUND RC COLUMNS CAN INCREASEDUCTILITY AND DISSIPATING ENERGY

The effectiveness of both thin high-strength RC jacketing system and CFRP jacketing system in improving the hysteretic performance of existing RC columns is experimentally and analytically investigated.
Critical parameters studied herein were the strengthening material, lap splice length (increased for CFRP-strengthened column), and amount of confinement provided by jackets.

Existing RC structures built prior to the 1960s-1970s are particularly vulnerable due to poor confinement and inadequate lap splices, leading to rapidly degrading hysteresis behavior dominated by brittle failure modes.

Conclusions In the present study, the effectiveness of two strengthening schemes in improving the overall hysteresis performance of RC columns with poor seismic details was experi‐ mentally and analytically investigated. Three column specimens of 1:1.5 scale were con‐ structed, designed for gravity loads only. The main structural deficiencies of the columns included the use of concrete with low compressive strength, plain steel reinforcement, widely spaced ties and inadequate length of the lap splices of reinforcement. Subse‐ quently, these specimens were enhanced by either wrapping layers of CFRP textile along the critical column height (specimen FS2) or by using high‐strength concrete to confine the critical region with a thin RC jacket (specimens RG1 and RG2). The strengthened columns were then subjected to a large number of incremental amplitudes of lateral displacement under constant axial loading, to s egion with a thin RC jacket (specimens RG1 and RG2). The strengthened columns were then subjected to a large number of incremental amplitudes of lateral displacement under constant axial loading, to simulate the equivalent effect of strong earthquake mo‐ tions. The examined variables were the strengthening material, the length of the lap splices and the amount of confinement provided by the jackets. Based on both the exper‐ imental data acquired during the seismic tests and the implementation of the proposed analytical formulation, a comprehensive analysis of the hysteresis response of the speci‐ mens was attempted. Moreover, the seismic behavior of the strengthened columns was further evaluated with respect to the cyclic performance of two corresponding original specimens, O1 and O2, and the response of a control one, C1, with continuous reinforce‐ ment, which were tested in a previous work [3]. It was clearly demonstrated that the thin RC jackets of high strength provided ade‐ quate confinement to the critical region of specimens RG1 and RG2, where the lap splices of reinforcement are located, and hence, satisfactorily improved the load transfer mecha‐ nism between the lap‐spliced bars. Meanwhile, premature lap splice failure and excessive bar slipping were effectively precluded. Consequently, the strengthening interventions applied to specimens RG1 and RG2 allowed for the development of the columns' nominal flexural moment capacities, while securing a ductile dissipating hysteresis behavior.
